extracted.intended_audience: college and university administrators, Title IX coordinators, campus legal counsel, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards for how recipients of federal funds (e.g., colleges and schools) must receive reports of sexual harassment, investigate and respond, provide supportive measures, classify mandatory reporters, and document decisions to avoid deliberate indifference under Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an "appropriate person" / "responsible employee" (who gives actual knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: An `appropriate person' or `responsible employee' is an official/employee who at a minimum has authority to address the alleged discrimination and to institute corrective measures; actual knowledge includes notice to any official who has authority to institute corrective measures on behalf of the recipient (including the Title IX Coordinator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Gebser and OCR guidance (e.g., 2001 Guidance at 13). Assessment of who qualifies should consider legal authority to redress harassment and the institution's own policies. Courts evaluate factual reality (e.g., teachers, principals, superintendents) rather than relying solely on titles. Avoid over-inclusive characterizations that label every employee a responsible employee without regard to authority to take corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual knowledge and what constitutes notice
rubrics_metrics.description: `Actual knowledge' includes notice to the Title IX Coordinator or any official of the recipient who has authority to institute corrective measures; notice is not limited to a particular channel and may include reports to other officials described in §106.8(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must recognize that actual knowledge can be established by reports to officials with corrective authority. The rule equates notice to such officials with the portion of OCR's prior definition of responsible employees who can take action to redress harassment. Because the scope depends on who has corrective authority, institutions should map roles and authority when assessing notice pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posting and accessibility of Title IX Coordinator contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must list and prominently display the Title IX Coordinator's office address, telephone number, and email on institutional websites and otherwise provide the contact information so any person may report sexual harassment at any time (including outside business hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.8(a) and §106.8(b) require prominent display and availability of contact information; reports can be made by mail, phone, email, or any method designated by the recipient (including online portals). Institutions should ensure contact information is easy to find and that mechanisms allow out-of-hours reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal complaint: definition and trigger for mandatory investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A `formal complaint' is a written document filed by a complainant or signed by the Title IX Coordinator requesting that the recipient investigate allegations of sexual harassment; once a formal complaint (including electronic submissions) is filed, §106.44(b)(1) obligates the recipient to investigate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.30 defines `formal complaint' and explicitly includes electronic submissions such as email or online portals if the recipient provides them. Institutions must have processes to accept and process written/formal complaints and to initiate investigations in response. The distinction between informal reports and formal complaints affects whether the grievance process is triggered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to respond when the school `should have known' (constructive knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under prior OCR guidance, a school has a duty to respond to harassment it reasonably should have known about (i.e., if it would have learned the harassment with reasonable care or a diligent inquiry), including situations where harassment is pervasive, openly practiced, or well-known to students and staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2001 Guidance (and earlier guidance) describes examples (hallway harassment, graffiti, harassment during teacher-supervised activities) where pervasiveness can demonstrate that a school should have known. The final regulations reference but do not reproduce that expansive `should have known' approach; institutions should be aware of the factual circumstances that might be construed as constructive notice and the practical consequences (e.g., triggering obligations to investigate). OCR materials have carved out some exceptions (see public awareness events discussion) but institutions should not assume a blanket safe harbor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures: definition, availability, and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures are individualized, non-punitive, non-disciplinary services designed to restore or preserve a person's equal access to education; recipients must offer supportive measures promptly upon actual knowledge and must provide them unless the complainant declines, and must document reasons if supportive measures are not provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.30 defines supportive measures; §106.44(a) requires prompt response and offering of supportive measures regardless of whether a formal complaint is filed. Examples include academic or housing changes, no-contact directives, counseling referrals (the pre-2017 guidance called similar steps `interim measures'). §106.45(b)(10) requires documentation explaining why the recipient's response was not deliberately indifferent and, specifically, why supportive measures were not provided if applicable. Recipients must ensure supportive measures do not unreasonably burden the other party and are available to both parties when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim measures vs supportive measures and equal availability
rubrics_metrics.description: What earlier guidance called `interim measures' (e.g., separating students, housing changes) are characterized in the final regs as `supportive measures' to signal that such services must be offered whether or not a formal grievance is pending; schools must not make such measures available only to one party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare 2001 Guidance and 2011 Dear Colleague Letter (which used the term `interim measures') with §106.30 and §§106.44–106.45. The final rule emphasizes that supportive measures are available even absent a grievance process, and 2017 Q&A reiterates that interim/supportive measures should not be available only to one party. Institutions should review policies to ensure equitable availability and that supportive measures are not conditioned on filing a formal complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation standards: promptness, thoroughness, and impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations must be prompt, thorough, and impartial; the specific steps depend on nature of allegations, source of complaint, age of parties, institutional size/structure, and other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2001 Guidance at 15–18 and the Dear Colleague Letter stressed prompt, thorough, impartial inquiry and that steps will vary by context. Institutions should design investigative processes reflecting these standards and be prepared to tailor procedures to particular circumstances while maintaining impartiality and sufficient thoroughness to resolve allegations and to support documentation obligations under §106.45(b)(10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate indifference / standard of institutional response
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient's response is evaluated under a `not clearly unreasonable in light of the known circumstances' standard (deliberate indifference); recipients must take actions to restore and preserve equal access and avoid responses that are clearly unreasonable, while retaining discretion for responses not specified in the regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble contrasts OCR's prior language about `effective corrective actions' with the final regs' deliberate indifference standard. 2001 Guidance framed effectiveness by a reasonableness standard; the final rule codifies `not clearly unreasonable' as the general liability metric but also requires compliance with specific regulatory obligations. Institutions must meet regulatory requirements and document the rationales for responses, balancing reasonableness and institutional discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary decision-making: proportionality and educational impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary sanctions must be made to enforce the institution's code of conduct while considering the impact of separating a student from education; any disciplinary decision must be proportionate to the violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 2001 Guidance, 2011 Dear Colleague Letter, and 2017 Q&A stating that disciplinary actions (counseling, warnings, discipline) may be appropriate but should be proportionate and consider educational disruption. Institutions should weigh sanctions' effect on access to education and ensure sanctions are not imposed in a way that unduly infringes on due process or academic continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of mandatory reporters (wide‑net reporting) and exceptions for confidential roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must carefully classify which employees are mandatory reporters; `wide-net' or universal mandatory reporting (designating virtually all employees as reporters) has been criticized for undermining survivor autonomy and chilling disclosures; counseling/confidential roles should be exempted from mandatory reporting obligations that identify the student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly critiques (Weiner, studies of campus policies) document the growth of broad mandatory reporting and the harms (reducing disclosures, undermining agency, secondary victimization). 2014 Q&A exempts responsible employees with counseling roles from identifying students. Institutions should limit reporter designations to those students reasonably expect to have authority to redress violence, exclude confidential resources, and consider special categories (RAs, campus police, coaches) through thoughtful policy design, balancing survivor autonomy with institutional obligations and exceptions for minors or imminent safety risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality requests, weighing factors, and when to proceed despite a complainant's wishes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a complainant requests confidentiality or requests that the complaint not be pursued, the school should take reasonable steps to investigate and respond consistent with that request but must weigh factors (including whether due process or safety concerns preclude confidentiality) and may, in some circumstances, initiate a grievance process despite the complainant's wishes—such a decision must be reached by the specially trained Title IX Coordinator and be documented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2001 Guidance, 2011 DCL, and 2014 Q&A provide that confidentiality requests limit the school's ability to pursue discipline if due process requires disclosure; schools should consider a range of factors when weighing confidentiality (2014 Q&A). The final regulations respect complainant autonomy but permit initiation of grievance processes when necessary; recipients must document the reasons why proceeding was not deliberately indifferent and the Title IX Coordinator must have communicated with the complainant about their wishes. Institutions should establish clear protocols for evaluating confidentiality requests and documenting decision rationales.
